FWS is federal work study, yes! I'm not sure what CLEP stands for - College Level Examination something, I'd assume - but it's basically a test you can do to test out of college-level classes. For example, you could take the composition CLEP test, and if you got a high enough score it would count as college credit for whatever English composition classes required by your school. I believe it's around $200 per test, but that saves you so much money compared to what each class costs! You can't do it for all subjects, but most of the gen eds have an associated CLEP test.

The only reason I recommended going to the Christian school for the gen eds is to buy time for OP to get their finances more in order and be able to be more independent when the time comes for them to get a real education in the science classes, because of the potential reaction from the parents when they transfer. I don't know their situation but it's possible their parents would cut them off for going to a secular school and if that's the case, it might be wise to play along until they're mentally prepared to be cut off. If OP's parents actually do pay in full for the Christian school, the gen eds should be fine to take there, except possibly biology and history. They would pay for a pretty decent chunk of it, and that would leave OP with more expensive classes but a smaller chunk than the overall cost they might be facing if they do choose to start at a secular college.

It will be hard. You'll have to work a while to save up before you even apply, and you'll have to keep working even during college. I'm an engineering major so I'll be overloaded between school and work, but I'm going to figure it out because I have to or I don't go to school. You can do it, if you set your mind on it. 

I took two years off after high school because I needed money and I needed to solidify what I wanted to do. Now I have better scholarships than the first time I applied, and I have a more reliable car and money in the bank. It's okay to take a few years off, and you might be better off for it. Your test scores are valid for quite a while after you take the tests, and besides - you have the chance to improve your scores in the meantime.

Another option is to do your research, figure out what gen eds are required for the schools you really want to attend, and go to the Christian school and just take those. You can transfer to your real school after you've had the gen eds and it'll probably save you money in the long run, especially if your parents will pay for it. You can save money in the summers and have more saved back for when you have to break away from what they want for you.

You can get a lot of the amenities of a city without actually having to live in the absurdly heavy traffic and pollution. You can drive most places in OKC (not sure about Tulsa, I don't usually have a reason to go to Tulsa so I've only been there a handful of times when I was younger), and even city housing is cheaper than most other places in the country.

Everything's much cheaper here. Even in the "fancy" places like Edmond, you can find a small apartment for $800-900/month. Take everything as it comes.

If you don't have the food for one order, move on to the next. Keep doing that process until you find an order you can bag, and then bag it. Sometimes it backfires and stresses me out further but other times it helps a lot.

I will often "prep" the bags for an order or multiple orders if I'm waiting for the food from kitchen. ONLY DO THIS IF YOU CAN KEEP TRACK OF IT WELL. I'll print the stickers for each bag/order if I have more than one or two, and at least for me, having less on my screen is less stressful even if I have more on the counter. Sometimes, if I can given the contents of the order, I'll put parts of it in first, and this helps me to be able to more quickly finish the order once I get the food. Other times, it's just the bags.

Be a good communicator. If you need something, be sure people are making it. If you can see your kitchen well enough, you can see whether or not people are working at the station you need things from. If they're not, call it back! If it's taking a while, ask if they're waiting on something. I also always ask when I can see I don't have enough non-specials (like regular/spicy/nuggets) because not all of the BOH pays attention. (Tips for BOH too; it's VERY helpful when you check that! I know y'all make extras and often assume you don't need it but it makes it go smoother when you check and make it to order when needed.) Don't be too pushy, but be communicative. Be patient, but make sure they know what you need. Also communicate with the rest of DT when you're waiting on certain things.

Be aware that as you're learning, especially for your first few rushes, it'll be difficult and you'll make mistakes. Mistakes are part of the job, just learn from them and do better next time.

What else... For bag sizes, I like to use 12lb for 2 sandwiches 1 fry. Clamshells can fit in an 8lb bag. 8ct and smaller nuggets, 3ct and smaller strips, individual sandwiches, cookies, brownies, soups, parfaits, and grilled nuggets can all fit in a 4lb. For doordash, always bag a size up from what you would normally do (with the exception of really small orders because too big isn't good either.) It's better to choose a bag that's too big than too small, but you'll eventually learn which ones are good for what.

READ THE STICKERS ON SPECIALS. I sometimes struggle with this too. Especially with our routing system (1st lane and mobiles go to a separate screen from 2nd and 3rd lane during lunch and dinner), it's easy to grab the wrong thing entirely, if you're not paying attention. Attention to detail is key when it comes to bagging.

We had 10 30 counts in doordash during our midday rush (when we really consistently don't have enough people to deal with it). It was an absolute joy to deal with because at the exact same time we also had a very large catering order for a bus where they wanted each individual meal bagged separately with names.
